source.title: The Geometry of Refusal: Why Post-Hoc Safety Is Fragile and Pretraining-Time Safety Persists
source.authors: Srikanth Malla; Chi-Ho Choi; J. Choi

record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream capability-probe NLLs at several model sizes, a different measurement from fitted scaling laws. It does not fit or test the original power-law procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Chinchilla and discusses compute-optimal training budgets as context, but reports no held-out pretraining-loss scaling sweep, fitted power laws, or extrapolation tests. Table 20 reports LM-only probe NLLs at four sizes; these bear on V6. Co-training capability-cost comparisons and refusal-rate scale results do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: A safety-geometry paper (post-hoc refusal fragility, substrate emergence, co-training). It cites Chinchilla only to place token budgets. It fits no loss scaling law and makes no scaling claim. Table 20's LM-only base NLLs at four sizes are a by-product of the co-training cost comparison, not a scale test. Every size uses a fixed 10B tokens, so larger models are increasingly under-trained (a fourteenth of Chinchilla at 6.9B). The learning rate is not retuned, there is one run per size, and no uncertainty is given for base levels. The authors say ARITH variation is unresolvable run-to-run variance. These points cannot show whether downstream performance scales predictably.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but misses the main point. The authors conclude that post-hoc safety updates lie nearly orthogonal to capability Fisher directions (suppression), so benign fine-tuning strips refusal by 35 to 38 pp. Refusal's representational substrate emerges between 1B and 63B tokens in OLMo-2-1B. Continuous safety co-training through pretraining yields refusal that erodes only 2 to 14 pp from 410M to 6.9B, at a small cost on short-answer probes. They draw no scaling-law conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Reports probe NLL across model sizes rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss scaling laws or predicting larger runs.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe outcome varies with task: RECALL and INSTRUCT NLL decrease across the four sizes, while REASON has a slight final reversal and ARITH is non-monotonic. All size runs use 10B C4 tokens; the paper says this is short of compute-optimal from 1B upward.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 20: LM-only Pythia-architecture models (410M to 6.9B, fixed 10B C4 tokens) show RECALL and INSTRUCT gold-span NLL falling with size. REASON is flat (about 4.5) and ARITH is non-monotone (8.59, 7.97, 8.34, 8.46).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed, sub-compute-optimal token budget, downstream gold-answer NLL need not fall monotonically with parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: App. I: capability-gradient norm across pretraining is U-shaped. It is smallest near the compute-optimal tokens/param ratio on Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-2-1B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability-loss gradient norm is minimised near the Chinchilla-optimal token ratio during pretraining.

record.code_released: Full code is stated to be in supplementary material; URL not stated.
record.problems: Only four model sizes and four capability probes are reported for this relevant scale sweep. The authors state that larger models are under-trained at the fixed 10B-token budget; no scaling fit, uncertainty for the LM-only NLL values, or prediction test is provided.
record.rows_left_out: Table 20 also reports co-training cost relative to the LM-only base for each probe and size. Those are intervention-specific capability-cost results, not measurements of downstream performance scaling or predictive fit. Other refusal-rate and co-training results do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining-loss sweep or power-law fit.
No other modality or regime scaling fit.
No designed test of downstream predictability with scale or loss. The incidental Table 20 sweep is confounded by fixed tokens and single runs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels were built on an incidental, confounded size sweep: fixed 10B tokens, untuned lr, single runs. The authors explicitly say ARITH is unresolvable. I reclassify the study as T6 with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token allocation trend.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other-modality or alternate-training-regime scaling-law test.
No fit linking downstream performance to scale or pretraining loss, and no prediction or extrapolation test.
No comparison of scaling-law fit choices or exponents; mentions of Chinchilla are contextual rather than a test.
